summary: This best current practice says native apps should make OAuth 2.0 authorization requests only through external user agents, mainly the user's browser, and not through embedded web views. It explains the security and usability reasons and how apps and servers can follow it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8252 says an installed app must not draw its own login form. It must send the user to the browser, let the user sign in there, and bring the result back to the app through a URI the app registered. Servers must offer three ways of receiving that URI, and apps must add a one-time secret to the request so that a code stolen by another app cannot be used.

subtitle: Why a mobile app should send the user to the browser to sign in, and how to bring the answer back.

tldr.problem: An app that shows its own sign-in page can read the user's password and cookies, and forces the user to sign in again for every app.
tldr.mechanism: The app opens the system browser for the authorization request and receives the reply through a redirect URI it registered with the operating system. Public native app clients must use PKCE, so an intercepted authorization code is useless.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8252 is BCP 212 and updates RFC 6749. It is also known as the AppAuth pattern, after the open-source libraries that implement it.

facts.label: PKCE for native apps
facts.value: Required for public native app clients

today: RFC 8252 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 212, and updates RFC 6749; no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. The extension it depends on is RFC 7636, Proof Key for Code Exchange.

sections.title: Why the Browser and Not the App
sections.content:
Section 9 of the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework documents two approaches for native apps to interact with the authorization endpoint: an embedded user-agent and an external user-agent. This best current practice requires that only external user-agents like the browser are used for OAuth by native apps, and documents how native apps can implement authorization flows using the browser as the preferred external user-agent, as well as the requirements for authorization servers to support such usage. This practice is also known as the AppAuth pattern, in reference to open-source libraries that implement it.

For authorizing users in native apps, the best current practice is to perform the OAuth authorization request in an external user-agent, typically the browser, rather than an embedded user-agent such as one implemented with web-views. Previously it was common for native apps to use embedded user-agents, and that approach has many drawbacks, including the host app being able to copy user credentials and cookies, as well as the user needing to authenticate from scratch in each app.

Native app authorization requests that use the browser are more secure and can take advantage of the user's authentication state. Being able to use the existing authentication session in the browser enables single sign-on, as users do not need to authenticate to the authorization server each time they use a new app, unless required by the authorization server policy.

Supporting authorization flows between a native app and the browser is possible without changing the OAuth protocol itself, because the OAuth authorization request and response are already defined in terms of URIs, and this encompasses the URIs that can be used for inter-app communication. Some OAuth server implementations that assume all clients are confidential web clients will need to add an understanding of public native app clients and the types of redirect URIs they use.
sections.plainLanguage: The reason is both security and convenience. A page drawn inside the app can read what the user types and can copy the session cookies, and the user has to sign in again for each app. A real browser keeps its own secure session, so the user signs in once and the app never sees the password.

sections.title: The Terms Used Here
sections.content:
A native app is an app or application that is installed by the user on their device, as distinct from a web app that runs in the browser context only. Apps implemented using web-based technology but distributed as a native app, so-called hybrid apps, are considered equivalent to native apps for the purpose of this specification. An app store is an e-commerce store where users can download and purchase apps.

An external user-agent is a user-agent capable of handling the authorization request that is a separate entity or security domain to the native app making the request, such that the app cannot access the cookie storage, nor inspect or modify page content. An embedded user-agent is a user-agent hosted by the native app making the authorization request that forms part of the app or shares the same security domain, such that the app can access the cookie storage and/or inspect or modify page content. The browser is the default application launched by the operating system to handle http and https scheme URI content.

An in-app browser tab is a programmatic instantiation of the browser that is displayed inside a host app but that retains the full security properties and authentication state of the browser. A web-view is a web browser user interface component that is embedded in apps to render web pages under the control of the app. Inter-app communication is communication between two apps on a device.

A claimed https scheme URI is a URI that some platforms allow apps to claim after proving ownership of the domain name; URIs claimed in such a way are then opened in the app instead of the browser. A private-use URI scheme is, as used by this document, a URI scheme defined by the app following the requirements of Section 3.8 of RFC 7595 and registered with the operating system, such that URI requests to such schemes launch the app that registered it to handle the request. Reverse domain name notation is a naming convention based on the domain name system, but where the domain components are reversed, for example app.example.com becomes com.example.app.
sections.plainLanguage: The distinction that matters is whether the app can see what the browser does. If it can, the app is an embedded user-agent and is not allowed. If it cannot, it is an external user-agent and it is fine.

sections.title: The Authorization Flow in the Browser
sections.content:
Just as URIs are used for OAuth 2.0 on the web to initiate the authorization request and return the authorization response to the requesting website, URIs can be used by native apps to initiate the authorization request in the device's browser and return the response to the requesting native app. By adopting the same methods used on the web, the benefits seen in the web context, such as the usability of a single sign-on session and the security of a separate authentication context, are gained in the native app context too. Reusing the same approach also reduces implementation complexity and increases interoperability by relying on standards-based web flows that are not specific to a particular platform.

The interaction has six steps. The client app opens a browser tab with the authorization request. The authorization endpoint receives the request, authenticates the user and obtains authorization, which may involve chaining to other authentication systems. The authorization server issues an authorization code to the redirect URI. The client receives the authorization code from the redirect URI. The client app presents the authorization code at the token endpoint. The token endpoint validates the authorization code and issues the tokens requested.

To conform to this best practice, native apps must use an external user-agent to perform OAuth authorization requests. This is achieved by opening the authorization request in the browser and using a redirect URI that will return the authorization response back to the native app.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange is the familiar web one, with the app standing in for the website. The app asks the browser to open the authorization request, the user signs in there, the browser is handed a short code and passes it back to the app, and the app swaps the code for an access token at the token endpoint.

sections.title: Starting the Request and Receiving the Reply
sections.content:
Native apps needing user authorization create an authorization request URI with the authorization code grant type, using a redirect URI capable of being received by the native app. The function of the redirect URI for a native app authorization request is similar to that of a web-based one: rather than returning the authorization response to the OAuth client's server, the redirect URI used by a native app returns the response to the app.

Public native app clients must implement the Proof Key for Code Exchange extension to OAuth, and authorization servers must support PKCE for such clients. After constructing the authorization request URI, the app uses platform-specific APIs to open the URI in an external user-agent. Typically the external user-agent used is the default browser, that is, the application configured for handling http and https scheme URIs on the system; different browser selection criteria and other categories of external user-agent may be used. This best practice focuses on the browser as the recommended external user-agent, and an external user-agent designed specifically for user authorization and capable of processing authorization requests and responses like a browser may also be used. Other external user-agents, such as a native app provided by the authorization server, may meet the criteria set out in this best practice, including using the same redirection URI properties, but their use is out of scope.

Some platforms support a browser feature known as in-app browser tabs, where an app can present a tab of the browser within the app context without switching apps, but still retain key benefits of the browser such as a shared authentication state and security context. On platforms where they are supported, it is recommended, for usability reasons, that apps use in-app browser tabs for the authorization request.
sections.plainLanguage: The app builds a normal authorization request, adds a secret it keeps to itself, and hands the whole thing to the browser. The app also tells the server where to send the answer, using one of three kinds of address that the operating system can route back to it.

sections.title: Three Ways to Receive the Redirect
sections.content:
To fully support this best practice, authorization servers must offer at least the three redirect URI options described in this section to native apps, and native apps may use whichever option suits their needs best, taking into account platform-specific implementation details.

Private-use URI scheme redirection is the first option. Many mobile and desktop platforms support inter-app communication via URIs by allowing apps to register private-use URI schemes, sometimes colloquially referred to as custom URL schemes, such as com.example.app. When the browser or another app attempts to load a URI with a private-use URI scheme, the app that registered it is launched to handle the request. When choosing a URI scheme, apps must use a URI scheme based on a domain name under their control, expressed in reverse order. For example, an app that controls the domain name app.example.com can use com.example.app as its scheme. A scheme such as myapp would not meet this requirement, as it is not based on a domain name. When there are multiple apps by the same publisher, care must be taken so that each scheme is unique within that group. As there is no naming authority for private-use URI scheme redirects, only a single slash appears after the scheme component, so a complete example is com.example.app:/oauth2redirect/example-provider.

Claimed https scheme URI redirection is the second option. Some operating systems allow apps to claim https scheme URIs in the domains they control, and when the browser encounters a claimed URI the native app is launched with the URI supplied as a launch parameter, instead of the page being loaded in the browser. Such URIs are indistinguishable to the authorization server from a regular web-based client redirect URI, with an example of https://app.example.com/oauth2redirect/example-provider. As the redirect URI alone is not enough to distinguish public native app clients from confidential web clients, it is required that the client type be recorded during client registration. These redirects have some advantages compared to the other options in that the identity of the destination app is guaranteed to the authorization server by the operating system, so native apps should use them over the other options where possible.

Loopback interface redirection is the third option. Native apps that are able to open a port on the loopback network interface without needing special permissions, typically those on desktop operating systems, can use the loopback interface to receive the OAuth redirect. Loopback redirect URIs use the http scheme and are constructed with the loopback IP literal and whatever port the client is listening on: http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{path} for IPv4 and http://[::1]:{port}/{path} for IPv6, with the example http://127.0.0.1:51004/oauth2redirect/example-provider. The authorization server must allow any port to be specified at the time of the request for loopback IP redirect URIs, to accommodate clients that obtain an available ephemeral port from the operating system at the time of the request. Clients should not assume that the device supports a particular version of the Internet Protocol, and it is recommended that they attempt to bind to the loopback interface using both IPv4 and IPv6 and use whichever is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ways back. The app can register a private address with the operating system, it can claim an https address in a domain it owns, or on a desktop it can open a port on its own machine. The last one is the weakest, because other programs on the machine can also reach that port.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The redirect URI options share the benefit that only a native app on the same device, or the app's own website, can receive the authorization code, which limits the attack surface. Code interception by a different native app running on the same device may still be possible. A limitation of private-use URI schemes is that multiple apps can typically register the same scheme, which makes it indeterminate which app will receive the code. Loopback IP-based redirect URIs may be susceptible to interception by other apps accessing the same loopback interface on some operating systems. App-claimed https scheme redirects are less susceptible to URI interception due to the presence of the URI authority, but the app is still a public client and the URI is sent using the operating system's URI dispatch handler with unknown security properties.

The PKCE protocol was created specifically to mitigate this attack. It is a proof-of-possession extension to OAuth 2.0 that protects the authorization code from being used if it is intercepted: the client generates a secret verifier, passes a hash of this verifier in the initial authorization request, and must present the unhashed verifier when redeeming the authorization code. An app that intercepted the authorization code would not be in possession of this secret, rendering the code useless. Authorization servers should reject authorization requests from native apps that do not use PKCE by returning an error message.

The OAuth 2.0 implicit grant authorization flow generally works with the practice of performing the authorization request in the browser, but as the implicit flow cannot be protected by PKCE, its use with native apps is not recommended. Access tokens granted via the implicit flow also cannot be refreshed without user interaction, making the authorization code grant flow, which can issue refresh tokens, the more practical option for native app authorizations that require refreshing of access tokens.

Other risks are addressed as follows. For loopback redirects, clients should open the network port only when starting the authorization request and close it once the response is returned, and should listen on the loopback network interface only, in order to avoid interference by other network actors. The use of localhost is not recommended, because specifying the loopback IP literal rather than localhost avoids inadvertently listening on network interfaces other than the loopback interface, and is less susceptible to client-side firewalls and misconfigured host name resolution.

For client impersonation, the authorization server should not process authorization requests automatically without user consent or interaction, except when the identity of the client can be assured. This includes the case where the user has previously approved an authorization request for a given client id: unless the identity of the client can be proven, the request should be processed as if no previous request had been approved. Measures such as claimed https scheme redirects may be accepted by authorization servers as identity proof.

For fake external user-agents, the advantage of everyone using external user-agents is that it is possible for security experts to detect bad actors, as anyone faking an external user-agent is provably bad; if good and bad actors alike were using embedded user-agents, bad actors would not need to fake anything, making them harder to detect.

For cross-app request forgery, it is recommended that native apps include a high-entropy secure random number in the state parameter of the authorization request and reject any incoming authorization responses without a state value that matches a pending outgoing authorization request.

For authorization server mix-up attacks, a unique redirect URI is required for each authorization server used by the app, for example by varying the path component, and authorization responses must be rejected if the redirect URI they were received on does not match the redirect URI in an outgoing authorization request. The app must store the redirect URI used in the authorization request with the authorization session data and must verify that the URI on which the authorization response was received exactly matches it.

Finally, embedded user-agents must not be used to perform authorization requests. They are unsafe for use by third parties by definition, as the app that hosts the embedded user-agent can access the user's full authentication credential, not just the OAuth authorization grant intended for the app. In typical web-view-based implementations the host application can record every keystroke entered in the login form, automatically submit forms to bypass user consent, and copy session cookies and use them to perform authenticated actions as the user. Even when used by trusted apps belonging to the same party as the authorization server, embedded user-agents violate the principle of least privilege. Aside from the security concerns, they do not share the authentication state with other apps or the browser, requiring the user to log in for every authorization request.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is that another app on the device steals the code. The defence is PKCE: the app sends a hash of a secret it made up, and has to show the secret itself when it swaps the code for a token, so a stolen code is worthless. The rest of the section deals with fake browsers, apps pretending to be the app you meant, and one server tricking another.

sections.title: Registering Native Apps and What Servers Must Support
sections.content:
Except when using a mechanism like Dynamic Client Registration to provision per-instance secrets, native apps are classified as public clients and must be registered with the authorization server as such. Authorization servers must record the client type in the client registration details in order to identify and process requests accordingly.

Authorization servers must require clients to register their complete redirect URI, including the path component, and reject authorization requests that specify a redirect URI that does not exactly match the one that was registered. The exception is loopback redirects, where an exact match is required except for the port URI component. For private-use URI scheme-based redirects, authorization servers should enforce the requirement that clients use schemes that are reverse domain name based; at a minimum, any private-use URI scheme that does not contain a period character should be rejected. Requiring a scheme based on a domain name that is under the control of the app can also help to prove ownership in the event of a dispute where two apps claim the same private-use URI scheme: if two apps claimed com.example.app, the owner of example.com could petition the app store operator to remove the counterfeit app, and such a petition is harder to prove if a generic URI scheme was used. Authorization servers may also request the inclusion of other platform-specific information, such as the app package or bundle name.

Secrets that are statically included as part of an app distributed to multiple users should not be treated as confidential, because one user may inspect their copy and learn the shared secret. For this reason it is not recommended for authorization servers to require client authentication of public native app clients using a shared secret, as this serves little value beyond client identification which is already provided by the client_id request parameter. Servers that still require a statically included shared secret for native app clients must treat the client as a public client and not accept the secret as proof of the client's identity.

The server support checklist at the end of the document lists five things an OAuth server that supports native apps must do: support private-use URI scheme redirect URIs, which is required to support mobile operating systems; support https scheme redirect URIs for use with public native app clients, used by apps on advanced mobile operating systems that allow app-claimed https scheme URIs; support loopback IP redirect URIs, required to support desktop operating systems; not assume that native app clients can keep a secret; and support PKCE, which is required to protect authorization code grants sent to public clients over inter-app communication channels.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has to know that this client is an app and not a website, so it can apply the right rules: no shared secret to protect, exact match on the redirect address, and a secret code proof on every request.

viz.caption: THE ATTACKS AND WHAT ANSWERS THEM

items.title: Code interception
items.text: PKCE: the app must present the secret it generated, so an intercepted code is useless.

items.title: Client impersonation
items.text: Record the client type at registration, and require user consent unless the client's identity can be proven.

items.title: Fake external user-agents
items.text: An app that fakes one is provably bad, so it can be detected and blocked.

items.title: Cross-app request forgery
items.text: Put a high-entropy random number in the state parameter and reject responses that do not match.

items.title: Authorization server mix-up
items.text: Use a unique redirect URI per server and reject a response that arrives on a different one.

items.title: Embedded user-agents
items.text: Not allowed: the host app can read the password and copy the session cookies.
